sentence: An 84-year-old man with a personal history of allergy to procaine and streptomycin, underwent left hip replacement and bilateral inguinal hernia.
In August 2010 he was diagnosed with PR and treatment with prednisone 30 mg/day was indicated.
The patient was independent in activities of daily living and had no cognitive impairment.

At the time of consulting the Nephrology Service (8 months after RP was diagnosed), he was on therapy with prednisone 5 mg, omeprazole 20 mg/day, enalapril 5 mg every 12 hours, levothyroxine 25 mg/day, chlorthalidone 12, 5 mg/day.
The patient was admitted to the Nephrology Service due to an increase in volume in the lower limbs and the abdomino-scrotal region for four days.
During the interrogation he only reported a slight decrease in the rate of diuresis and nocturia all at once.

The physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 150/80 mmHg, heart rate of 80 bpm, globular abdomen with dullness in the mesogastrium and pitting edema in the lower limbs, with the rest of the examination being unremarkable.
Blood tests upon admission showed: creatinine: 0.8 mg/dl; cholesterol: 354 mg/dl; triglycerides: 104 mg/dl; albumin: 2.2 g/dl; Total proteins: 5 mg/dl.
The blood count and coagulation were normal.
Hepatitis B, C and human immunodeficiency virus serology: negative.
In the immunological study, antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and complement was normal.
IgG was 450 mg/dl (normal range: 751-1560) and IgM and IgA were normal.
Blood electrophoresis showed a percentage decrease in albumin without monoclonal peaks.
Tumor markers (carcinoembryonic antigen [CEA], CA19-9, alpha-fetoprotein, and prostate-specific antigen [PSA]) were within normal values.
CA125 of 136 IU/ml (normal value: 0-35).
Protein quantification in 24-hour urine was 9.51 g/24 h.
Creatinine clearance, 77 ml/min.
Urine electrophoresis also ruled out the presence of monoclonal peaks, with Bence-Jones proteinuria being negative.
The chest x-ray revealed a right pleural effusion.
In the renal ultrasound, the kidneys were 11 cm in size and there were no stones or dilation.
An abdominal computed tomography scan was performed, which revealed thickening of the gastric folds.
For this reason, a gastroscopy was requested, which confirmed the existence of a thickened pyloric fold, but without evidence of malignancy in the pathological study.

Given the presence of a florid nephrotic syndrome, an ultrasound-guided percutaneous renal biopsy was performed with the findings: «5 glomeruli per section plane, all of them with usual histological characteristics.
Immunofluorescence was negative for the markers studied (IgG, IgA, IgM and C3).
"Both the interstitium, the tubules and the vascular component had no lesions."
The final diagnosis was minimal change nephropathy (MCN).
Based on the biopsy findings, the prednisone dose was increased to 1 mg/kg/day.
One month later, in the outpatient clinic, remission of the clinical and biochemical nephrotic syndrome was confirmed and a descending prednisone regimen was indicated.

Seven months later, when the patient was on maintenance therapy with prednisone 5 mg/day, a relapse of nephrotic syndrome was observed, which forced the dose of prednisone to be increased to 50 mg/day.
After the disappearance of the nephrotic syndrome, a decreasing prednisone regimen was indicated until reaching a dose of 2.5 mg/day.
One month after maintaining prednisone at a dose of 2.5 mg/dl, the patient consulted his primary care physician due to edema.
The analysis confirmed the appearance of proteinuria of 1.66 g/day, so it was decided to increase the dose of prednisone to 10 mg/day, achieving the disappearance of proteinuria.
In the last Nephrology review, on maintenance with prednisone 10 mg/day, the patient was asymptomatic and without proteinuria.
